section.title: Sequences as limits indexed by whole numbers
section.p: Limits so far have used a real input approaching a point (x\to a or x\to\infty). But many approximations arrive step by step. Bisection produces successive intervals; decimal approximations add digits one by one.
The input is a counting number n=1, 2, 3, \ldots. A limit of such an ordered list is a limit of a sequence.

statement.p: A sequence is a function whose domain is the set of positive integers. We denote its outputs by subscripts: a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots, a_n, \ldots, where a_n is called the nth term.
Let x_1=1 and x_{n+1}=\frac{x_n+2}{2}. The sequence begins:
Each term moves halfway from the current value to 2.
We write \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=L if for every \varepsilon\gt 0, there exists a positive integer N such that whenever n\ge N, we have
If such a finite real number L exists, the sequence is called convergent. Otherwise, it is divergent.
Let \varepsilon\gt 0 be given. Choose an integer N\gt \frac{1}{\varepsilon}. For all n\ge N, we have n\gt \frac{1}{\varepsilon}, so \frac{1}{n}\lt \varepsilon. Thus |\frac{1}{n}-0|\lt \varepsilon.
Divide numerator and denominator by n:
A sequence (a_n) is increasing if a_{n+1}\ge a_n for all n, and decreasing if a_{n+1}\le a_n for all n. A sequence is monotone if it is either increasing or decreasing.
A sequence is bounded above if a_n\le B for all n, bounded below if a_n\ge A for all n, and bounded if both hold.
Let a_n=1-\frac{1}{n}. Since a_{n+1}-a_n = \frac{1}{n(n+1)}\gt 0, it is strictly increasing. Since a_n\lt 1 for all n, it is bounded above by 1. It converges to 1.

figure.caption: The sequence a_n=1-1/n increases toward 1 without passing it.

statement.p: Every increasing sequence that is bounded above converges.
Every decreasing sequence that is bounded below converges.

proof.p: Let (a_n) be increasing and bounded above. The set of values S=\{a_n : n\in\mathbb{N}\} is bounded above, so by the completeness of the real numbers, it has a least upper bound L=\sup S.

Given \varepsilon\gt 0, L-\varepsilon is not an upper bound, so there is some N with a_N\gt L-\varepsilon. Because (a_n) is increasing, for all n\ge N we have L-\varepsilon\lt a_N \le a_n \le L, meaning |a_n-L|\lt \varepsilon. Hence \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n = L.

subsection.title: Bisection as a sequence
subsection.p: The bisection method produces two sequences: the left endpoints (L_n) (increasing, bounded above) and the right endpoints (R_n) (decreasing, bounded below).
Since the interval length R_n-L_n = \frac{R_1-L_1}{2^{n-1}} \to 0, both sequences converge to the same trapped root c.

subsection.title: Sequences as preparation for infinite series
subsection.p: An infinite series \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n is defined as the limit of its sequence of partial sums s_N = \sum_{n=1}^N a_n.

statement.p: For \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\cdots, the partial sums are s_N = 1-\frac{1}{2^N}. As N\to\infty, \frac{1}{2^N}\to 0, so \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n}=1.

warning.title: Terms tending to zero does not guarantee convergence
warning.p: a_n\to 0 is necessary for \sum a_n to converge, but not sufficient. For example, \frac{1}{n}\to 0, yet \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n} (the harmonic series) diverges.

subsection.p: Sequences bridge static limits to dynamical processes. If secant slopes \frac{f(a+1/n)-f(a)}{1/n} settle toward one number as n\to\infty, they reveal the instantaneous rate of change: the derivative.
